articleTitle: WASPNET-a wavelength switched photonic network for telecommunication transport
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: WASPNET is an EPSRC-funded collaboration between Strathclyde, Essex, and Bristol Universities, with the aim of designing a flexible packet-based transport network. It supports both conventional optical paths for the transport of SDH and also switches optical packets, thus providing a smooth upgrade path from SDH over WDM while still supporting legacy SDH equipment. A key feature of this network is the use of multiple wavelengths to help resolve packet contention and hence reduce the size of optical buffers that are required. This is advantageous since large optical buffers will be expensive and difficult to build. This paper describes some of the developments in WASPNET. Two possible control architectures have been studied, namely scattered wavelength path (SCWP) and shared wavelength path (SHWP). SCWP is the most suitable as it can distribute the load more efficiently and it requires a lower buffer size. Two possible node designs are then addressed; one based on feedback delays and one on feed forward delays, followed by a description of the sub-system components and their advantages and limitations. Finally the decoding of subcarrier modulated headers is covered.

articleTitle: Design issues in compact optical switches using spatial light modulators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: Optical switches are likely to play an important role in WDM networks for use in network protection. For undersea networks it is essential that the devices are compact and hence thermally stable. Compact optical switches using spatial-light modulators can be implemented using a diffractive lens. In this paper we investigate the performance implications of such a switch architecture.

articleTitle: All-optical routing using a 12/spl times/12 passive InP wavelength selective router and tuneable wavelength conversion
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: All-optical routing of 2.5 Gbit/s WDM signals across two cascaded optical cross connects (OXCs) with a penalty of only 0.6 dB has been demonstrated using tuneable wavelength converters and a passive WDM router.

articleTitle: Transmission limitations in optical WDM networks due to cross-phase modulation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: High power optical amplifiers and dispersion management enable increased length of inter-amplifier spans in multi-channel high bit-rate transmission systems. The bit-rate-distance product is limited by the combined effects of fibre dispersion and non-linear effects due to the high launched power into the fibre. In a dispersive fibre, the combined effects of self-phase modulation (SPM), cross-phase modulation (XPM) and four-wave mixing (FWM) affect the transmission performance. Phase modulation due to XPM has a significant influence on a WDM system as it affects channels over a continuous wavelength range and is converted into amplitude distortion by residual dispersion. Little work has been done investigating the XPM induced pulse distortion systematically in dependence of a wide range of parameters. We present an experimental and theoretical investigation of an XPM impaired system depending on fibre dispersion, channel wavelength spacing, bit-rate and pulse form. Excellent agreement has been found between the experimental and computer simulation results.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: WDM systems are being installed as a means to realise higher capacity, however, most of these WDM networks have an individual channel capacity of up to 2.5 Gbit/s. Initially WDM systems based on 4 wavelengths were deployed, 16 wavelength systems are now readily available with 32 wavelengths and above becoming available with further expansion planned. The maximum number of possible wavelengths is currently limited by the optical amplifier bandwidth. Based on the ITU channel spacing of 100 GHz and today's state of the art optical amplifiers a maximum of approximately 40 channels can be envisaged, giving a maximum transmission capacity of 100 Gbit/s at 2.5 Gbit/s per channel. In order to increase this capacity further it will be necessary to raise the individual channel bit rates beyond 2.5 Gbit/s. Alternatively reduced channel spacing can be used although this will require enhanced component specification and reduced system performance tolerance, this will therefore increase overall system cost. We explain the implementation of a 32 wavelength system where the single channel bit rate can be up to 10 Gbit/s. Although much higher bandwidths have been achieved in the laboratories this 320 Gbit/s capacity is at the leading edge in terms of public network transmission systems.

articleTitle: BT's WDM trial-integrating WDM into an existing network
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: BT is introducing WDM into its core network with two pilot schemes due to carry live traffic from 1998 summer. These are unique in that they employ 1+1 optical multiplex section protection and are capable of carrying both PDH and SDH traffic. In order to ensure that the WDM system does not degrade the performance of the traffic carried over it BT is undertaking full integration testing of the WDM systems with its existing transmission systems. This is providing valuable experience and an understanding of optical network issues.

articleTitle: Optimised wavelength-set multi-stage broadband access network employing arrayed-waveguide grating routers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: We present a novel 3-stage multi-Gb/s switched ATM access architecture, which requires only 24 wavelengths, spaced by 1.6 nm to route to up to 6912 customers. A multi-dimensional bi-directional addressing strategy, based on spatial, wavelength and temporal multiplexing, is adopted, by exploiting the functionality of cascaded programmable and passive arrayed-waveguide gratings (AWGs). Symmetric upstream and downstream bandwidths are enabled by taking advantage of the optical reciprocity of input and output AWG ports, and their cyclic-shifting properties. The outside-plant consists of only passive, temperature-insensitive components, and the requirement for stable and accurately-defined wavelength sources is avoided, so reducing overall costs. The architecture maps onto 99% of current UK network topology, and allows an elegant evolutionary path from current passive optical networks (PONs).

articleTitle: A technique for wavelength converting a 2.488 Gb/s signal whilst simultaneously monitoring and replacing a wavelength identifying pilot tone
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: We investigate the use of a single integrated semiconductor optical amplifier (SOA)/distributed feedback DFB) laser to perform both all-optical wavelength conversion and simultaneous pilot tone replacement/monitoring at the SONET/SDH bit rate of 2.488Gb/s (STM-I6). It is also demonstrated that reamplification and reshaping regeneration of the optical signal is possible under certain conditions.

articleTitle: All optical wavelength conversion at 2.488 Gbit/s using the integrated multi grating cavity (MGC) laser
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: A novel integrated multi-wavelength grating cavity (MGC) laser has been used for multi-channel wavelength conversion at 2.488 Gbits/s. Functions demonstrated include conversion to multiple wavelengths, WDM multiplexing and 1/spl times/4 space switching.

articleTitle: Non-linear phase apodisation techniques for arrayed-waveguide grating passband control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: The authors have presented a series of novel techniques for improving the passband flatness of arrayed-waveguide gratings (AWGs). Either phase or complex amplitude functions are used to produce the required broadening without excessive compromise on the intrinsic wavelength selectivity. Minimum passband variance parameters for both the phase and complex techniques have been shown, the latter producing a near-ideal trapezoidal passband characteristic.

articleTitle: Transmission of densely-spaced 10 Gbit/s WDM channels using a dispersion-compensated, amplified recirculating fibre loop and concave grating demultiplexer
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: Successful transmission, in a recirculating loop, of 4/spl times/10 Gbit/s with 50 GHz channel spacing, over dispersion compensating fibre has been demonstrated. We investigated reductions in the maximum transmission distance due to SPM and cross phase modulation (XPM) by varying the optical launch power and also by comparing multi-channel and single channel transmission performance. We have shown that precompensation results in compression of the shorter pulses, which enables an increase in the transmission distance, as predicted by simulations reported previously.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: This paper presents a technical description of the SeaMeWe3 submarine WDM system. This multiple owner system will provide large capacity between 40 countries in SE Asia, the Mediterranean and Western Europe. The system is not only using WDM, but also breaking new ground through the use of submerged wavelength add drop multiplexers (WADMs).

articleTitle: Wavelength routing for advanced optical networks
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Multiwavelength Optical Networks: Devices, Systems and Network Implementations (Ref. No. 1998/257)
abstract: Wavelength division multiplexing (WDM) is a reality for optical transmission systems with many vendors offering solutions with 16, or more, channels at bit rates of up to 10 Gb/s. These systems are essentially static and point-to-point, with the WDM providing a cost effective way to increase capacity. The challenge now is to capitalise on the move beyond WDM and find new ways in which network features can be expanded whilst cost is reduced. This paper focuses on the following areas: the effect of different market segments, a possible evolutionary path for adding functionality in the optical layer of the network, the role of management in the optical network, and a description of an experimental wavelength router developed by Nortel.
